lesson.title: The General Recipe: From Table Cells to Conditional Probability
lesson.summary: Every conditional distribution calculation follows the same underlying rule, that a conditional proportion equals a joint proportion divided by a marginal proportion, the same logic behind the formal definition of conditional probability.
lesson.body:
Every conditional distribution you compute, no matter which row or column it comes from, follows the exact same two-step recipe. First, identify the condition, the group you are restricting attention to, and find its total. Second, divide the count for the category you care about by that condition's total, not by the grand total of the whole table. Turning this into an explicit habit, always naming the condition and its total out loud before dividing, prevents the single most common error in this topic: accidentally dividing by 300 when you should have divided by 120. This same recipe works no matter how many rows or columns the table has, and no matter whether the condition happens to be a row category or a column category.

This recipe is really just the two-way-table version of the formal definition of conditional probability: P(A given B) equals P(A and B) divided by P(B). Here P(A and B) is the joint proportion, the count in one specific cell divided by the grand total, and P(B) is the marginal proportion, the row or column total divided by the grand total. When you divide a cell count directly by a row total, as in the conditional distribution section, you are computing this same ratio, just with the grand total canceling out of both the numerator and denominator along the way. Seeing both versions side by side is useful because some problems hand you proportions or probabilities directly, without ever showing you the underlying counts, and in those cases the formula is the only route available.

Take P(iPhone given Freshman) from the 300-student survey. The quick method divides the cell count by the row total: 70 iPhone-using freshmen divided by 120 total freshmen equals 0.5833, or 58.3 percent. The formula method instead converts everything to proportions of the grand total first: P(iPhone and Freshman) equals 70 divided by 300, which is 0.2333, and P(Freshman) equals 120 divided by 300, which is 0.4. Dividing these, 0.2333 divided by 0.4, gives 0.5833, or 58.3 percent again. Both methods agree exactly, because they are the same calculation written two different ways.

Direction matters enormously here, and reversing it changes the answer. P(iPhone given Freshman) asked what fraction of freshmen use an iPhone, giving 58.3 percent. The reversed question, P(Freshman given iPhone), asks what fraction of iPhone users are freshmen, using the iPhone column total of 160 as the denominator instead: 70 divided by 160 equals 0.4375, or 43.75 percent. These are two legitimately different numbers answering two different questions, and mixing them up is a common and consequential mistake.

Getting this recipe automatic, correctly naming the condition, finding its total, and dividing the matching count by that total, is what makes the next step possible: comparing conditional distributions across several groups reliably enough to draw a real conclusion about whether two categorical variables are associated.
